Suppose we have a pair of parallel lines cut by a transversal.

Alternate interior angles are the pairs of angles on alternate (opposite) sides of the transversal and are interior to (inside of) the parallel lines. These pairs of angles always have equal measure.

[IMG: /graphics/bf21a54ed421cd7695b04a55b35a6b29]

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that [MATH: \angle{BAF}] and [MATH: \angle{AFC}] are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal [MATH: \overleftrightarrow{AF}] cuts the parallel lines [MATH: \overleftrightarrow{AB}] and [MATH: \overleftrightarrow{CF}.] Hence,

[MATH: m\angle{AFC} = m\angle{BAF} = 70^{\circ}\,.]

Also, notice that [MATH: \angle{FBE}] and [MATH: \angle{BFC}] are alternate interior angles formed when the transversal [MATH: \overleftrightarrow{BF}] cuts the parallel lines [MATH: \overleftrightarrow{AB}] and [MATH: \overleftrightarrow{CF}.] Hence,

[MATH: m\angle{BFC} =m\angle{FBE} = 110^{\circ}\,.]

Now, using the angle addition postulate, we can find [MATH: \angle{AFB}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: m∠AFB|= m∠BFC − m∠AFC; = 110^{∘} − 70^{∘}; = 40^{∘}]
